newsitem.title: USA: PORK - High prices squelch US shoppers' appetites.
newsitem.headline: PORK - High prices squelch US shoppers' appetites.

text.p: Supermarket shoppers shocked by the unusually steep rise in pork prices this summer may have to wait until next year before finding price relief on bacon, hams and pork chops, analysts and meat dealers said.
An unexpected cutback in U.S. hog production early this year and a sharp increase in pork exports to Japan this summer combined to drive hog and pork prices sharply higher.
Pork output is now on the rise and wholesale prices are rapidly falling but it may be several months before supplies are sufficient to push supermarket prices significantly lower.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture last week reported average pork prices reached an all-time high in September of $2.34 a lb while bacon prices also jumped to a record high price of $2.81 a lb.

"I wouldn't expect pork prices to rise as fast in the next couple of months as they did the past eight months. But, we don't have enough pork yet to push prices down," said Joseph Uhl, a food marketing economist at Purdue University.
Uhl said the average U.S. bacon price jumped to $2.81 a lb in September from $2.14 in January which he said was "one of the fastest-rising food prices in grocery stores."

Prices for pork chops and hams also rose during that period. Richmond, Va.-based Richfood Holdings Inc, which supplies more than 1,000 supermarkets on the Atlantic coast, estimated high prices cut sales of bacon and pork chops this summer by 15 percent.
"We just haven't had the opportunity to feature the pork loins like we have been," said Mike Baker, vice president of meat procurement at Richfood.
Baker said it may be another month before bacon can be advertised at a low enough price to boost sales.

Chuck Levitt, livestock analyst with Chicago-based Alaron Trading Corp, said some of the reasons for the high pork prices can be traced back to 1995, when a poor U.S. corn crop sent prices for corn and other livestock feeds sharply higher. This caused hog producers to reduce herds from late 1995 to the spring of 1996.
"We had some very, very high prices for corn in the fall and winter of 1995," said Levitt.

Coinciding with this drop in pork production was a 95-percent increase in pork exports to Japan from January to August, 1996 versus a year ago. Japan is the leading export market for U.S. pork, although exports have slowed since the summer.
"We moved a horrendous amount of stuff. We took it away from our market and sent it to Japan," said Levitt.
The latest U.S. Agriculture Department figures show year-to-date 1996 pork production is down about four percent from a year ago.
